turns.doctor_question: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Hi, Doctor. Thank you for seeing me. I... well, it's a bit hard to know exactly where to start, because it feels like a lot of little things have been building up, but lately, in my role—I'm a medical services manager, so I oversee a clinic and handle a lot of the administrative and operational side of things—it's just gotten to a point where I really can't ignore it anymore. 

You see, there's just so much data we have to track nowadays, and I have my degree in this, I know how to do this, I've been doing it for years. But what finally pushed me to actually make this appointment and come in today is that I will sit down at my desk to start an EPIC quality report, and I have every intention of tracking it. I tell myself, okay, we are going to focus and get this done. Or I'll sit down in one of our clinic metrics meetings with the department heads. And within just a few minutes... my mind has drifted so incredibly far away. I'll suddenly snap back and realize I'm just rereading the exact same column of numbers over and over again on my screen, or I'm sitting in the meeting and I've completely missed the entire point of the discussion. 

It's incredibly frustrating because I am sitting right there. I'm looking right at the monitor, or right at the presenter, nodding along, and my brain is just... somewhere else entirely. I'll be thinking about a totally different project, or what I need to pick up on the drive home, or just nothing at all, and then I have to scramble to catch up, hoping nobody notices that I just blanked out for five minutes while they were talking about patient throughput times. It's just exhausting having to constantly fight my own brain just to pay attention to the things I actually need to be focusing on.

symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient describes an inability to sustain attention on tasks like writing reports or sitting in meetings, with their mind drifting after just a few minutes.
symptom_reasoning.S003: The patient mentions sitting in meetings, looking right at the presenter and nodding along, but completely missing the point of the discussion because their brain is elsewhere.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient notes being distracted by unrelated thoughts, such as thinking about a different project or what to pick up on the drive home during tasks and meetings.
symptom_reasoning.S059: The patient explicitly states they have 'blanked out for five minutes' and struggle to focus, indicating difficulty concentrating and their mind going blank.

turns.doctor_question: How long have you been experiencing these difficulties with concentration and attention? Has this been something you've dealt with since childhood or school, or is this something that's developed more recently?
turns.patient_response:
Well, that's an interesting question, because, you know, when I really sit down and think about it... it's not like I've always been this way. I mean, I got my bachelor's degree, I made it through school, and I've been working in medical administration for a long time. I always had my little systems, you know? Color-coded folders, specific routines for checking emails, sticky notes in very specific places on my monitor. And that worked. It really did. But then... well, it was exactly two years and four months ago. I know the timeline perfectly because it was right after the fiscal year ended in October, and the clinic director pulled me into his office and offered me this promotion. It was a huge step up, a much larger portfolio. Suddenly I wasn't just managing one small department's workflow; I was overseeing multiple clinics, integrating their data, handling these massive EPIC reports that pull from dozens of different providers. 

And at first, I was so excited, but almost immediately, it was like... my systems just broke. The sticky notes and the color-coding just weren't enough to hold the dam together anymore. The sheer volume of information just overwhelmed everything I used to rely on to keep myself on track. So, to answer your question, no, it wasn't childhood. It really started right around that promotion, two years and four months ago, when the workload just expanded beyond what my old tricks could manage. And ever since then, it's just been this constant, uphill battle every single day to try and force my brain to stay locked onto the data in front of me.

symptom_reasoning.S005: The patient notes that their previous organizational systems 'broke' and they are now overwhelmed and unable to keep themselves on track with the larger workload.

turns.doctor_question: Outside of work—when you're at home, spending time with family or friends, or doing personal activities—do you notice the same kinds of attention problems, or is it mainly something that happens at work?
turns.patient_response:
Well, you know, it's funny you ask that, because I've spent so much time agonizing over how this is impacting my job that I almost didn't realize how much it was bleeding into everything else until recently. But yes, absolutely, it's happening outside of the clinic too, and it's... it's really starting to become a problem in areas of my life that used to bring me a lot of joy. 

For instance, I've been involved for years with these volunteer health workshops in my community. We set up little weekend clinics, do blood pressure screenings, health education, that sort of thing. I used to be the one organizing the logistics, coordinating the volunteers, getting all the supplies together. I loved doing it. But lately... I've actually had to step back from leading those planning committees. I just can't reliably keep all the pieces moving anymore. I would sit down at home on a Saturday morning with my coffee, open up the volunteer roster, and just... stare at it. I'd start thinking about the flyers, and then I'd wonder if I emailed the venue, and then I'd realize I hadn't even finished reading the first email from a volunteer, and an hour would go by and I'd have accomplished absolutely nothing. It got to the point where I was dropping the ball, and I felt so guilty that I finally had to tell the board I needed to take a lesser role. 

And at work, it's not just that I'm frustrated with myself—it's actually starting to impact other people now, which is what really keeps me up at night. Because of these delays, because I can't just sit down and power through an EPIC report like I used to, I'm starting to miss clinic reporting deadlines. And in my role, when I miss a deadline, it creates this whole bottleneck. Other teams are literally sitting around waiting on me to get them the data they need to do their jobs. The finance department will be waiting on my throughput metrics to finalize their quarterly projections, and I'll be sitting at my desk, practically in tears, trying to force my eyes to just read the numbers on the screen so I can hit send. It's just... it's everywhere now. It's not just me being annoyed with my own brain, it's actually stopping me from functioning the way I need to, both professionally and personally.

turns.doctor_question: When you're sitting at your desk trying to focus on those reports, or in meetings, do you find yourself feeling physically restless or fidgety? Do you have trouble sitting still, or do you feel this urge to move around or do something with your hands?
turns.patient_response:
You know, it's actually the exact opposite, which is maybe why it took me so long to realize there was a real problem here. I mean, I don't have that... that physical need to get up and pace around or anything like that. In fact, if you were to look through the glass wall of my office—we have these glass partitions that look out over the administrative floor, which is a whole other issue with visual distractions, but anyway—if you were to look at me while I'm trying to work on those EPIC reports, I probably look like a statue. 

And in meetings, especially the big quarterly reviews with the department heads... we usually hold those in the main conference room on the third floor, the one with the really heavy, oversized leather chairs. I'll sit there, and my hands will be perfectly folded on the table, or maybe I'll have a pen in my hand resting on my notepad. I'm not tapping the pen, I'm not shaking my leg, I'm not shifting around in my seat. I've always prided myself on having very good professional posture, you know? It's important in a management role to project a certain calm, grounded presence, so I'm very aware of how I physically present myself. 

So, physically, I am completely stationary. I can sit in that chair for two hours straight without feeling the slightest urge to stand up or stretch or fiddle with my jewelry. It's almost like my body is completely locked in place, doing exactly what it's supposed to be doing. But inside... inside my head, that's where all the movement is happening. It's like my brain just got up, walked out the door, went down to the hospital cafeteria, started thinking about the menu, and then wandered out into the parking lot to check the weather. 

So no, I really don't feel restless in my body at all. I don't have that urge to move my hands or feet. It's just my focus that won't sit still. I'll just be sitting there, staring blankly at the screen or the presenter, perfectly quiet and still, while my thoughts are a million miles away. It's funny, really, because my husband is a leg-bouncer, you know, whenever we watch TV his knee is just going a mile a minute, and I always thought *that* was what having trouble focusing looked like, but for me, it's entirely invisible from the outside.

turns.doctor_question: When you're trying to focus on work and your mind drifts away, do you notice yourself feeling anxious or worried about not being able to concentrate, or do you experience any physical tension—like tightness in your chest, neck, or shoulders—during these episodes?
turns.patient_response:
Anxious or worried... well, it's interesting you phrase it that way. Because you'd think I would be, right? With all those deadlines looming and the other departments waiting on me. But when I'm actually in the middle of it, when my mind is doing that drifting thing? No, not at all. It's actually incredibly quiet. 

I don't get that tight feeling in my chest, and my neck and shoulders don't tense up. I mean, sure, my neck gets a little stiff sometimes just from staring at dual monitors all day—we upgraded to these massive double screens in administration last spring, which are supposed to be better for the workflow, but honestly it just means you're craning your neck back and forth for eight hours straight—but that's just normal desk fatigue, you know? It's not tension from losing my focus. 

When I'm sitting there and my brain just sort of... floats away from the data, I'm not panicked. I'm not gripping the mouse or clenching my jaw or anything like that. I'm usually just completely relaxed and totally lost in whatever random thought took over, like mentally re-organizing my kitchen pantry or trying to remember the name of that one billing specialist who retired three years ago. There's no physical tension at all. I don't even realize I'm not concentrating. The frustration only hits me *after* the fact, when I finally snap back to the present, look at the clock, and realize forty-five minutes have vanished and I haven't typed a single number. But during the actual drifting? No, I don't feel anxious or physically tight. It's just... a blank space where my attention should be.

turns.doctor_question: When your mind is drifting away from your work, does it feel like your thoughts are moving quickly from one thing to another—like they're racing or jumping around—or does it feel more like your thoughts are just sort of... blank or slow, like your brain has kind of shut down?
turns.patient_response:
Hmm. Racing or blank... honestly, I don't think I'd use either of those words. I've heard people talk about racing thoughts, like their brain is a television flipping through channels at lightning speed, but for me, it's really not like that at all. And it's definitely not shut down or blank, either. I'm not just sitting there with an empty head, staring into the void like a zombie. 

It's more like... well, let me think of a good example. Just the other day, I was supposed to be reviewing the compliance logs for the new sanitation protocols—which, by the way, the state just updated again, so we've had to revamp the entire checklist for the environmental services team, and it's been a massive headache because nobody wants to do the extra paperwork and I'm the one who has to enforce it. But anyway, I was looking at the spreadsheet, and my mind didn't go blank, and it wasn't racing. It just sort of... calmly walked away. 

I started thinking about whether I needed to buy more of those specific velvet hangers for my closet because I'm trying to reorganize my winter coats. And I just sat there, very peacefully, thinking about the dimensions of my closet, and whether the cedar blocks I bought last year were still good, and if I should maybe go to The Container Store this weekend because they usually have a sale around this time of year. It was a very normal, steady pace of thought. Just... completely the wrong thoughts for a Tuesday morning at the office. 

So, no, I wouldn't say it's a million miles an hour, and it's definitely not a blank screen. It's just a very detailed, very casual detour that I don't even realize I've taken until I look back at the compliance logs and realize I've spent twenty minutes mentally measuring my hallway closet. It's almost like my brain is functioning perfectly fine, at a perfectly normal speed, it's just decided to work on a completely different project than the one right in front of me.

turns.doctor_question: Do you find yourself acting on impulses without thinking things through, or do you interrupt people in conversations? Or do you struggle with doing things impulsively that you later regret?
turns.patient_response:
Impulsive? Oh, goodness, no. No, not at all. Honestly, if you were to ask anyone in my department, they’d probably tell you I’m the exact opposite. I am very, very measured. If anything, I probably take too long to make a decision because I want to look at all the angles. 

Take the new scheduling software we rolled out last fall, for example. The vendor wanted us to just jump right in and go live by October, and a lot of the clinic directors were pushing for it because the old system kept crashing during peak intake hours—which, honestly, was a server issue, not a software issue, I tried to explain that to IT, but you know how that goes when departments get siloed and refuse to communicate. Anyway, I didn't just impulsively sign off on the transition. I spent three weeks reviewing the implementation timeline, checking the data migration protocols, making sure the training modules were actually accessible for the older staff members who aren't as tech-savvy. I never do anything on a whim, especially not at work, but really not in my personal life either. 

And as for interrupting people... no, definitely not. I actually find it incredibly frustrating when people do that. In my role, I have to facilitate a lot of interdepartmental meetings, and there's this one chief of surgery—I won't name names, but he's been here for twenty years and thinks he runs the entire hospital—and he constantly talks over the nursing managers. It drives me absolutely up the wall. I always make it a point to let people finish their sentences. It's just basic professional courtesy, you know? It's crucial for maintaining morale.

So, no, I don't blurt things out, I don't make snap decisions I regret later, and I certainly don't interrupt. I’m perfectly content to sit there and listen quietly. The only problem, like I was saying before, is that while I'm sitting there so politely letting them finish their thought, my brain might have completely checked out of the conversation to think about grocery lists or staffing budgets. But as far as acting on impulse or jumping in to cut people off? No, I don't struggle with that at all. I'm very controlled.

turns.doctor_question: Have you ever had periods in your life—whether as a child, in school, or even as an adult—where you felt like you had a lot of excess energy, or where people commented that you seemed unusually active or 'hyper'? Or has it always been more about the attention piece without that energetic component?
turns.patient_response:
Excess energy? Oh, definitely not. No, it has always, always been just the attention piece. I have never been described as hyper in my entire life. Honestly, if you looked at my report cards from when I was a little girl in elementary school, every single teacher wrote the exact same thing: "A pleasure to have in class, very quiet, but daydreams frequently," or "Needs to focus on the task at hand." I was never the kid running around the classroom or acting out. My mother used to say I was her easiest child because I would just sit in the corner of the living room for hours. I mean, she thought I was reading, but half the time I was probably just staring at the same page for forty minutes thinking about what it would be like to live in a treehouse or something. But physically? Very still. 

And it's the exact same way now as an adult. I don't have any of that physical restlessness. If anything, I'm probably too sedentary. In my role, I am literally sitting at a desk or sitting in a conference room from eight in the morning until sometimes six at night. I can sit in the exact same ergonomic chair for three hours straight without even twitching. 

Like last month, for example, we had our quarterly budget review with the finance committee. That meeting is always a total marathon, usually four or five hours of just agonizing over line items, which is especially stressful this year with the new reimbursement rates changing how we have to forecast the fourth quarter. Anyway, the CFO was pacing around the room the whole time. He's one of those people who is always tapping his pen, shaking his leg under the table, getting up to pour a new cup of coffee every fifteen minutes. I remember watching him and thinking how absolutely exhausting it must be to carry around all that nervous energy. 

I don't experience that at all. I am perfectly content to sit completely still. The problem isn't that my body needs to move, it's just that my mind refuses to stay in the room. So while I'm sitting there looking like the most attentive, calm person at the conference table, mentally I'm completely gone, trying to remember if I took the chicken out of the freezer to thaw before I left for work. So, no, definitely no excess energy or hyper... anything. Just the drifting.

turns.doctor_question: When you're doing something that really interests you or captures your attention—whether it's a hobby, a personal project, or even something work-related that you find engaging—do you find that you can focus intensely for long periods of time, or do you have the same difficulty concentrating that you experience with the reports and meetings?
turns.patient_response:
Hmm. Intensely for long periods? Honestly... no, I don't think I do. I know some people can just lose themselves in a project for hours if they love it, but for me, it doesn't really seem to matter if it's a boring compliance report or something I actually genuinely want to be doing. The drifting happens anyway. 

Like, for example, outside of work, I really love gardening. I have this whole raised bed setup in my backyard that my husband helped me build three years ago—well, he built the wooden frames, I did all the soil mixing because I'm very particular about the compost-to-peat ratio, especially for the heirloom tomatoes since they can be so finicky with root rot. Anyway, I love it. It’s my absolute favorite thing to do in the spring. But even when I’m out there, doing something I supposedly enjoy, I can’t just focus on the gardening. I’ll be out there with my trowel, getting ready to plant the seedlings I’ve been babying indoors under grow lights for six weeks, and suddenly I’m just sitting on my knees staring at a pile of dirt because my brain has decided to wander off and think about the quarterly performance reviews I have to schedule for the administrative staff. 

Or even at work! Just last month, I volunteered to redesign the staff breakroom on the third floor. I was actually really excited about it because the old room was just completely miserable—awful fluorescent lighting, this peeling mustard-yellow linoleum from the nineties, and a microwave that always smelled like burnt popcorn. I had a decent little budget approved by the board to pick out new paint, comfortable chairs, and set up a nice little coffee station to try and boost morale. It was a really fun project! I love interior design. But I’d sit down at my desk with the furniture catalogs and the paint swatches, totally ready to dive in, and... ten minutes later, I haven't picked a single color because I'm mentally trying to remember if I sent a birthday card to my sister-in-law, or I'm wondering if I should switch my dog to a grain-free kibble. 

So, no, I wouldn't say I get locked in or intensely focused, even when I really care about the task. The subject matter doesn't seem to act as a... a glue, I guess, for my attention. My mind just takes its little casual strolls regardless of whether I'm looking at a budget spreadsheet or a seed catalog. It’s incredibly frustrating, to be honest, because you’d think the fun things would hold my interest, but they just don't. I just drift away no matter what I'm doing.

symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient confirms an inability to sustain attention for long periods, noting that their mind drifts even during enjoyable activities like gardening or design projects.

turns.patient_response:
Honestly, no. Like I was just saying, even in those moments where I really care about what I'm doing, my mind still wanders away. I never get that feeling of being completely absorbed or losing track of time because I'm just so focused. It's always the drifting. 

And, well... honestly, that inability to just stay present is exactly what finally pushed me to come in and make this appointment. Because it’s one thing when it happens with my tomatoes or picking out paint colors for a breakroom, but it’s happening with the things I absolutely cannot afford to drop the ball on. 

I can sit down at my desk to run an EPIC quality report—which, I don't know if you're familiar, but EPIC is our electronic medical record system, and the backend reporting module is just notoriously clunky, especially since the system-wide update they forced on us last quarter. But I will start that report, or I'll sit down in a crucial clinic metrics meeting with every single intention of tracking the information. I'll have my notebook open, my pen in my hand, completely determined to stay on top of the data. 

And then... I don't even know it's happening, but within just a few minutes, my mind has drifted so far off that when I finally snap back to reality, I realize I’m just staring at my monitor, rereading the exact same column of numbers over and over again without actually processing a single digit. Or I'll be in that metrics meeting and suddenly realize I completely missed the whole point of the discussion. The clinical director will look over at me for my input on patient throughput times or staffing adjustments, and I’ll realize I haven't heard a single word anyone has said for the last ten minutes. 

It’s just... it’s incredibly embarrassing, and it takes me twice as long to get my administrative work done because I have to keep starting over. So, no, I don't get captivated by things. The drifting just happens no matter how hard I try to prevent it, which is why I'm here.

turns.doctor_question: I want to ask you about something specific. Have you ever experienced a time—maybe just once or twice in your life—where you were doing something and you became so completely absorbed in it that hours passed without you even noticing? Where you looked up and realized it was suddenly much later than you thought?
turns.patient_response:
I know you’re trying to see if there’s maybe just one exception, but really... no. I feel like I'm repeating myself a bit, but I just don't have that gear. I never get that 'where did the time go' feeling because I was so locked into something. 

Even when I’m completely removed from work—like last summer, for instance. My husband and I rented this beautiful little house down in the Outer Banks for a week. We hadn't taken a real vacation in almost two years because of all the staffing shortages at the clinic, so I was absolutely determined to just unplug and relax. I brought this mystery novel that everyone in my neighborhood book club was absolutely raving about. It was supposed to be this gripping, unputdownable thriller, the kind of book you stay up until three in the morning reading. And I sat out on the deck, the weather was perfect, listening to the waves... but I just couldn't get lost in it. 

I'd read a page, and then I'd look at my watch. Then I'd read another page, and then I'd catch myself staring at a seagull for ten minutes, wondering if I remembered to set my out-of-office autoreply for both my internal and external emails, or if I only hit the internal one. Then I'd realize I hadn't absorbed a single word of the chapter and I'd have to start the page over. 

I am always, always acutely aware of the time passing, mostly because I'm constantly catching my mind wandering off and having to mentally drag my attention back to whatever is right in front of me. So, no, I've never had that experience where hours just vanish because I'm so deep into a task or a hobby. I honestly can't even imagine what that must feel like, to be that dialed into something. For me, every single hour feels like an hour, because I'm spending half of it just trying to keep my brain in the same place as my body.

turns.doctor_question: During the day, especially in the afternoon or during those long meetings, do you ever feel genuinely tired or sleepy? Like, do you ever struggle to keep your eyes open, or feel like your energy is just completely drained?

Sleepy? Hmm... no, not really. I mean, I know exactly the kind of feeling you’re talking about—that sort of mid-afternoon slump where your eyelids feel like they weigh ten pounds and you just want to put your head down on your desk. My husband gets that terribly, actually. If he doesn't have his second cup of coffee by two o'clock, he's practically nodding off in his home office by three-thirty. But for me? No, it’s not a physical tiredness at all.

My eyes are wide open. I'm never fighting off sleep or struggling to stay conscious. 

It’s... well, it’s not an energy issue. I feel perfectly fine physically. I don't feel drained or sluggish. It’s just that my attention is completely untethered. Like, I’ll be sitting there, fully alert, maybe even tapping my pen or shifting in my seat because I actually have all this pent-up energy from trying so hard to force myself to listen to the regional director drone on about Medicare billing updates, but my brain has just packed its bags and left the building. I'm awake, I'm just not *present*, if that makes sense. So, no, I wouldn't say I ever feel genuinely sleepy or drained during the day. It’s definitely not a lack of energy that's causing the problem.

symptom_reasoning.S029: The patient explicitly denies feeling physically tired, drained, sluggish, or lacking energy during the day.

turns.doctor_question: You mentioned gardening and interior design as things you enjoy. When you're researching or planning those projects—like looking up gardening techniques online, or reading about different plant varieties, or browsing design blogs—do you ever find yourself getting completely absorbed in that research to the point where you lose track of time, or does your mind still wander away from those topics too?
turns.patient_response:
Well, you’d think so, wouldn't you? Because it’s something I supposedly enjoy. Like, just last weekend I was trying to figure out the best companion plants for my Cherokee Purple tomatoes. They are notoriously finicky, by the way—they need just the right soil pH and really consistent watering or they split right down the middle before they even ripen. So I sat down with my iPad on the patio to read this one specific gardening blog that a master gardener in my neighborhood swears by. I had my coffee, the house was quiet, and I had every intention of just reading this one article about planting marigolds and basil near the tomato beds to deter pests. 

But even then... no. I don't get absorbed. I don't lose track of time at all. I’ll read maybe one paragraph about root systems, and then I’m suddenly thinking about whether I need to buy more garden twine, and then I’m looking at the patio furniture thinking the cushions need to be washed, and before I know it, my mind has just completely drifted away from the article. I end up reading the same sentence about soil drainage three times without it actually registering. 

And honestly, doctor, I know you were asking about my hobbies, but this is exactly why I was going on earlier about the clinic. I just keep coming back to it because it's what finally pushed me to come in and see you. If it was just the tomatoes, or if I just took three weeks to pick out a Sherwin-Williams paint swatch for the staff breakroom because I kept zoning out while looking at the design catalogs... well, I wouldn't be sitting in this chair right now. It’s frustrating, sure, but I could live with it. 

But like I was saying before, it’s the fact that this exact same drifting happens when I sit down to run those EPIC quality reports. It doesn't matter how high the stakes are. I will sit there in my office, or I'll be in one of those crucial clinic metrics meetings, with every single intention of tracking the information—knowing how vital it is for our quarterly compliance—and within just a few minutes, my mind has drifted so far that I’m just rereading the exact same column of numbers over and over. Or I'll snap back to reality in the middle of the meeting and realize I’ve completely missed the whole point of the discussion. It just doesn't matter if it's a hobby I love or a critical work task I absolutely have to do, my brain just will not stay put. So no, I never get completely absorbed, not even with the fun stuff.

symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient explicitly describes an inability to sustain attention during both leisure activities (reading gardening blogs) and work tasks (running reports, attending meetings), noting they frequently have to reread information.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient describes being easily distracted by unrelated thoughts and extraneous visual stimuli, such as suddenly thinking about garden twine or noticing patio cushions that need washing while trying to read.

turns.doctor_question: I want to ask you something a bit different. Have you ever in your life—even just once—experienced a time where you were so completely locked into doing something that you forgot to eat, or forgot to use the bathroom, or someone had to physically interrupt you because you didn't hear them calling your name? Even if it was just for an hour or two?
turns.patient_response:
Forget to eat? Oh, heavens no. I mean, I almost wish I could say yes, because it sounds like you'd be getting so much accomplished if you were that focused, but no, absolutely not. Actually, it's quite the opposite for me. 

Because my mind is constantly looking for an excuse to wander away from whatever I'm supposed to be doing, I am hyper-aware of every single physical sensation. If I am sitting at my desk—let's say I'm working on the annual budget reconciliation, which is just a nightmare of spreadsheets, by the way, because our different departments use three different software systems that simply refuse to communicate with each other properly, so I have to manually export and align all the data... anyway, if I'm doing that, and my stomach gives even the slightest little rumble, that's it. My brain completely abandons the spreadsheet. I'll spend the next twenty minutes thinking about what I should have for lunch, whether I should walk down to the hospital cafeteria on the first floor or if I should just eat the turkey sandwich I brought from home. I usually pack my lunches in these little glass containers now because my husband and I are really trying to reduce our plastic waste at the house, which is a whole project in itself. But before I know it, I'm thinking about recycling instead of the budget. 

And it's the exact same thing with using the restroom or hearing my name. I hear *everything*. If someone even walks past my office door, I look up. My assistant, Brenda—she's been with the clinic for fifteen years, absolute lifesaver, I don't know what I'd do without her—she always jokes that I have bat ears. She can just softly say my name from her desk out in the reception area, and I'll immediately drop what I'm doing and say, "Yes, Brenda, what do you need?" 

I am never, ever so locked into a task that I tune out the world around me. If anything, I'm practically begging the world to interrupt me so I don't have to use so much mental energy forcing myself to stare at my computer screen anymore. So no, I've never had a moment where I was so absorbed I missed a meal or didn't hear someone calling me. I just don't have that ability to block things out.

symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient describes their mind constantly wandering away from tasks and abandoning their work.
symptom_reasoning.S006: The patient states they hope for interruptions to avoid expending the mental energy required to focus on their computer screen.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient is easily distracted by minor physical sensations, unrelated thoughts about lunch and recycling, and extraneous noises like someone walking past their door.
symptom_reasoning.S003: The patient explicitly denies ignoring people when called, noting they hear everything and respond immediately when their assistant softly says their name.

turns.doctor_question: I want to make sure I understand this correctly. You're telling me that even with things you genuinely love—like your gardening or planning that breakroom redesign—you've never experienced even a single instance where you got so caught up in it that you looked up and realized several hours had passed without you noticing? Not even once, ever in your life?
turns.patient_response:
No, honestly, never. I know it sounds strange, because people always say time flies when you're having fun, but time never flies for me. It just crawls. 

I mean, take that breakroom redesign I was just talking about. I had this whole Saturday blocked out specifically for it a few weeks ago. My husband took the dogs to the park—we have two golden retrievers, absolute sweethearts, but they need so much exercise, otherwise they just pace around the kitchen island—so the house was completely empty and quiet. Perfect conditions, right? I had all the catalogs spread out on the dining room table, I had my little fabric samples for the new chairs, and I was trying to decide between these two paint colors, "Sea Salt" and "Rainwashed," because we really wanted to create a calming environment for the nursing staff. They are under so much stress right now with the new charting requirements that corporate rolled out last month, so I really wanted this room to be a sanctuary for them. 

So I sit down, I'm doing something I supposedly love, for people I care about, in a perfectly quiet house. And you would think I could just get lost in it for an afternoon. But I was checking the clock on the microwave every ten or fifteen minutes. I’d look at a blue-green swatch, and then I’d suddenly be thinking about whether the dogs were muddying up the back seat of my husband's car, and then I’d check my phone, and then I’d get up to water the pothos plant in the living room because I noticed a yellow leaf... and then I'd force myself back to the table. 

It's just this constant, exhausting cycle of starting and stopping. I never, ever have that feeling of, "Oh my gosh, where did the last three hours go?" It's more like, "How has it only been twelve minutes?" I am painfully aware of every single minute ticking by, no matter what I'm doing. So, to answer your question, no. Not once in my life have I ever been that absorbed in anything. I really wish I knew what that felt like, but I just don't.

symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient describes an inability to stay focused on a task she enjoys, experiencing a 'constant, exhausting cycle of starting and stopping' every 10 to 15 minutes.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient reports being easily drawn away from her task by unrelated thoughts (worrying about her dogs) and extraneous visual stimuli (noticing a yellow leaf on a plant).

turns.doctor_question: I want to ask you one more time about this, because it's really important. Has there ever been anything in your entire life—even something small, even something from when you were younger—where you sat down to do it and suddenly realized that four or five hours had gone by without you even noticing? Even if it only happened once?
turns.patient_response:
I know you keep coming back to this, doctor, and I... I really do understand why you're asking, because I know I must sound like a broken record here, but I promise you, I am racking my brain, going all the way back to when I was a little girl, and the answer is still just no. 

I mean, I remember when I was maybe ten or eleven, my mother bought me this massive jigsaw puzzle. It was a thousand pieces, a picture of the Neuschwanstein Castle in Germany. We have German heritage on her side of the family—her grandparents came over from Munich in the twenties—so she was always trying to get my brother and me interested in the culture. Anyway, she set it up on this folding card table in the den, thinking it would be this wonderful, immersive project for me over summer break. 

And I wanted to do it, I really did. It was a beautiful picture. But I would sit down at that wobbly little table, and I swear to you, I’d find maybe two edge pieces, and immediately I’d be wondering what the neighbor's dog was barking at outside. Or I'd start picking at the little vinyl covering on the corner of the card table, or I’d suddenly decide I absolutely needed a glass of lemonade right that very second. My mother used to get so exasperated with me. She’d say, "Can’t you just sit still and lose yourself in this for one afternoon?" But I couldn't. I'd look over at the grandfather clock we kept in the hallway, and it would literally have been seven minutes. Seven minutes, and I was already crawling out of my skin wanting to go do something else.

And it was the exact same way later on, like when I was in college getting my healthcare administration degree. My roommates would pull these intense all-nighters in the library, just completely buried in their anatomy or accounting textbooks for five or six hours straight, not even looking up. And I would be sitting right next to them, getting up to sharpen my pencil, and then going down to the vending machine for a Diet Coke, and then reading all the flyers on the bulletin boards in the hallway... I just had to piece my studying together in these agonizing little ten-minute increments. 

I just don't have that gear. I never have. My brain is always in a dozen different places at once, and because of that, I am always, always painfully aware of the time passing. I've never had a moment where four hours just vanished. I really wish I did! It sounds incredibly peaceful. But no, not even once.

symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient describes a lifelong inability to sustain attention on tasks, such as only being able to study in ten-minute increments or lasting only seven minutes on a puzzle.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient reports being easily distracted by extraneous stimuli, such as a dog barking outside or flyers on a bulletin board.
symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient mentions frequently getting up from their seat while studying to do unrelated things like sharpening a pencil or going to the vending machine.
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient describes feeling restless, stating they were 'crawling out of my skin wanting to go do something else' after just a few minutes of trying to sit still.

turns.doctor_question: Has there ever been a time when you absolutely had to complete something—maybe a deadline was looming, or someone was counting on you, or there was some kind of competition or stakes involved—where you found yourself completely locked in and unable to stop, even though you normally struggle to focus?
turns.patient_response:
I see what you're asking. Like, does the panic finally flip a switch in my brain and force me into the zone? And the answer is... no. It really doesn't. I mean, the panic is absolutely there, my heart will be pounding out of my chest, but it doesn't make me focus any better. If anything, the stress almost makes it worse. 

Just last year, for example, we had our triennial state health department inspection at the clinic. It is a massive, massive deal. If we get cited for major deficiencies, we could face huge fines or even risk our operating license, which means eighty people would be out of a job and hundreds of patients would have to scramble to find a new provider. The stakes literally could not be higher. And as the manager, I was the one responsible for making sure all the staff credentialing files were perfectly up to date before the surveyors walked through the door on Monday morning. 

I brought these three enormous, heavy banker's boxes of files home with me on Friday night. I knew I had to get through every single one of them. I was terrified. I knew people were counting on me. But did I get locked in? No. Not even close. 

I would open a folder—let's say it was Dr. Aris's file, he's our lead endocrinologist, brilliant man, truly, but just completely hopeless when it comes to keeping his paperwork compliant—and I'd see a missing signature on a training module from three years ago. And instead of just flagging it with a sticky note and moving to the next page like a normal person on a tight deadline, my brain would just... slip away. I'd suddenly be staring out the window wondering if I needed to clean the gutters before the spring rains started, or I'd realize my coffee was lukewarm so I'd go to the kitchen to microwave it, and while I was waiting for the microwave to beep I'd start reorganizing the spice rack because the cumin was in the wrong row... 

I was so panicked about the deadline the entire time, just sick to my stomach with anxiety, but I still couldn't string together more than ten or fifteen minutes of actual, continuous work. I never once got to a point where I couldn't stop. I was stopping constantly! I was looking for any excuse to stop. It took me the entire weekend, staying up until three in the morning both nights, just dragging my brain kicking and screaming back to those boxes a thousand different times. 

There was no flow. There was no locking in where the world melted away. It was just sheer, agonizing willpower mixed with absolute dread, and I was painfully aware of every single hour that ticked by on the clock. So even when the house is on fire, so to speak, I just don't have that gear. I really, truly don't.

symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient explicitly states they could not string together more than ten or fifteen minutes of continuous work, demonstrating difficulty sustaining attention.
symptom_reasoning.S006: The patient describes looking for any excuse to stop working and having to drag their brain 'kicking and screaming' back to the task, indicating a strong reluctance to engage in sustained mental effort.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient describes being easily distracted by unrelated thoughts and extraneous tasks, such as cleaning gutters or reorganizing a spice rack, while trying to work.

turns.doctor_question: Have you ever started doing something and found that you couldn't stop—like you kept going even though you wanted to take a break, or even though you knew you should stop and do something else? Where stopping felt almost difficult?
turns.patient_response:
I see what you mean, but no, absolutely not. Stopping is actually the one thing I am incredibly good at. I never have that feeling of being glued to a task where I cant tear myself away. If anything, I am always looking for an excuse to stop, even when I know I absolutely shouldn't. 

Like, every November, I have to do the annual performance evaluations for our administrative staff. We have twelve receptionists across our three clinic locations, and it is a tedious process, but it is so important for their annual raises. So I will sit down at my desk to write up the review for Sarah, who is our lead scheduler. She is a lovely girl, she actually just came back from maternity leave after having the sweetest little boy, so I really want to give her a thoughtful, detailed evaluation because she deserves it. 

But I will get maybe two sentences typed out about her phone etiquette, and immediately, stopping is all I can think about. I will think to myself, oh, my lower back is feeling a bit stiff, I should stand up and stretch. Or I will convince myself that I urgently need to go check the supply closet down the hall to make sure we have enough printer toner for the afternoon rush, which is completely ridiculous because we have an office manager who handles all the inventory and it has nothing to do with me. 

You are asking if I ever get stuck doing something and find it difficult to stop, but for me, it is the exact opposite. I can pull myself away from literally anything. I am practically begging my brain for a break every five minutes. My husband always jokes that I have a black belt in taking breaks. Even if we are watching a movie on a Friday night, a movie that I picked out, that I really wanted to see, I will pause it five or six times. I will tell him I am just going to get water, or I am just going to the kitchen to see if the dishwasher is done running. He will beg me to just sit and finish the film, and I want to, I really do, but I just cannot stay anchored to it. 

So no, I have never experienced a time where stopping felt hard or where I kept going when I wanted a break. I am like Teflon, honestly. Nothing ever sticks to me long enough for me to get trapped in it.

symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient describes a severe inability to sustain attention on both work tasks (writing evaluations) and leisure activities (watching a movie), needing a break every five minutes.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient is easily distracted by unrelated thoughts, such as suddenly needing to check the supply closet or the dishwasher while in the middle of a task or movie.
symptom_reasoning.S011: The patient frequently leaves her seat when she is expected to remain seated, such as getting up from her desk to stretch or check supplies, and repeatedly getting up from the couch during a movie.

turns.doctor_question: I want to ask you something very specific. Have you ever become so deeply absorbed in reading something—maybe a newspaper article, a work email, or even a text message from someone—that you read it over and over again without realizing you were rereading it, because you were so focused on understanding every detail?
turns.patient_response:
Oh, well, yes and no. Do I read things over and over again? Yes, constantly. But definitely not because I am deeply absorbed or focused on the details. It is actually the exact opposite. 

Honestly, doctor, that right there is what finally pushed me to come in and make this appointment. It has gotten to the point where I can start an EPIC quality report—we use EPIC for our electronic health records across all our clinics, and pulling those monthly compliance reports is a huge part of my job—or I'll sit down in a clinic metrics meeting with the department heads, with every intention of tracking the information. I will tell myself, "Okay, this is important, you need to pay attention to these patient throughput numbers." 

But within just a few minutes, my mind has drifted so far away. My eyes will literally be moving across the page or the screen, but absolutely nothing is registering in my brain. I will catch myself rereading the exact same row of numbers, or the exact same sentence in an email, four or five times in a row. And it’s not because I’m trying to deeply understand it, it’s because my brain just completely checked out and I have no earthly idea what I just read! 

It happens in those metrics meetings all the time, too. I’ll be sitting there, looking right at the presenter, nodding along, and then suddenly I kind of snap back to reality and realize I missed the whole point of the discussion. Someone will ask for my thoughts on the quarterly budget variances, and I’ll realize I haven't heard a single word anyone has said for the last ten minutes. It is incredibly embarrassing, especially at my level of management. I have to spend so much extra time at my desk just rereading the same reports over and over just to get a basic grasp of what they say, because my mind just refuses to stay on the page. So, yes, I reread things constantly, but it's because I'm drifting off, never because I'm absorbed.

symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient explicitly describes an inability to sustain attention on tasks like reading reports or attending meetings, noting their mind drifts away within minutes.
symptom_reasoning.S003: The patient describes sitting in meetings, looking directly at the presenter, but realizing they haven't heard a single word that was said.
